title: Aid programmes used as cover for spies
conviction: Three cases are on the public record, each exposed by accident. Whether the practice continues is the suspicion.
story: In 2011 a Pakistani doctor named Shakil Afridi went door to door in the town of Abbottabad offering hepatitis B vaccinations. The vaccination drive was run for the CIA, which was trying to find out who was living in the walled compound where Osama bin Laden was hiding. The suspicion this entry describes is that this was not a one-off: that the United States has used its aid programmes, over and over, as cover for intelligence work and political operations inside other countries. If so, people who accept a vaccine, a police-training course or a new phone service from a foreign aid agency cannot know who is really behind it, and the danger falls on genuine aid workers.

Three cases are documented. From 1962 to 1974 the US aid agency, USAID, ran an Office of Public Safety that trained and equipped police abroad; its director from 1962 to 1973, Byron Engle, is described in published histories as a CIA operative. By one historical count it sent about 1,500 advisers to at least 52 countries. Congress ended it in 1974, after Senator James Abourezk set out to expose its activities amid accusations that it taught torture. In 2014 the Associated Press revealed that USAID had built ZunZuneo, a text-message network for Cubans, through front companies in Spain and the Cayman Islands, paid through foreign banks. By USAID's own count it had about 68,000 users (AP had reported at least 40,000) before it shut down in September 2012, and users were not told who had made it. USAID said the programme was not covert. The third case is Abbottabad. Afterwards the deans of US public health schools wrote that seven or more United Nations workers vaccinating Pakistani children against polio had been shot dead, and in May 2014 the White House promised the CIA would make no operational use of vaccination programmes.

Each case came out by accident: congressional pressure in one, more than 1,000 pages of documents obtained by reporters in another, an arrest in Pakistan in the third. The 2014 promise covers vaccination and nothing else. The 1974 law that banned US training of foreign police had gained 'a dozen exemptions' by 1992, according to Senator Alan Cranston, whose remarks the Federation of American Scientists reproduces with a GAO report. No law requires the United States to say whether intelligence officers work under aid cover today. This map already carries the documented pattern on spy agencies, contractors and the lenders, built around John Perkins's account of US intelligence working through World Bank and IMF lending.

The question would be settled by the CIA's own records of how it used aid cover after 1974, the files the USAID inspector general opened on ZunZuneo in 2014, and the records on ZunZuneo that the Senate Foreign Relations Committee demanded from USAID that year, in a review that was also to compare it with programmes elsewhere. If those show that the three known cases were the whole of it, the suspicion fails.
missing: No count exists of intelligence use of aid cover after 1974. The USAID inspector general's 2014 file and the Senate Foreign Relations Committee records have not been located in published form.
would_settle: Declassified CIA records on use of aid cover after 1974; the USAID inspector general's 2014 ZunZuneo review; the records the Senate Foreign Relations Committee requested from USAID on ZunZuneo in 2014.

title: Forecasts inflated so countries borrow more
conviction: An insider's account, the World Bank's own 1992 review, a 245-dam study and an IMF working paper all find forecasts biased upward. Whether the bias is deliberate is the suspicion.
story: Before a country borrows to build a dam or a power grid, someone writes a forecast of what the project will cost and what it will earn. The suspicion is that these forecasts are pushed upward on purpose: costs written low and benefits written high, so the loan gets approved, the contractors get paid, and the borrowing country is left with the debt when the numbers never arrive. If that is true, part of the debt poor countries carry was built in from the first spreadsheet.

The best-known account comes from John Perkins, an economist at the Boston engineering firm Chas. T. Main in the 1970s, hired in 1971 as a junior economist and later, by his account, its chief economist. In a 2004 book he wrote that his job was to produce inflated growth forecasts so that countries would take large loans for projects built by US companies. Critics disputed many of his claims, above all that the National Security Agency was involved in hiring him. Einar Greve, the vice-president who hired him, at first backed the book's general account and later denied parts of it, including any link to the NSA.

Other records point the same way without relying on Perkins. In 1992 the World Bank's own Wapenhans report found that 37.5 per cent of the Bank's projects completed in 1991 were judged failures, up from 15 per cent in 1981. It blamed an "approval culture" in which staff treated project appraisals as a way to win approval, and found a growing bias toward over-optimistic expected returns. In 2014 an Oxford team, Atif Ansar, Bent Flyvbjerg and colleagues, studied 245 large dams in 65 countries built between 1934 and 2007. On average the dams cost 96 per cent more than budgeted, three in four ran over, and one of the authors, Atif Ansar, told International Rivers that dams backed by development banks did no better. The study names deliberate underestimating to win approval as one of the root causes. In 2020 an IMF working paper found the Fund's own growth forecasts too optimistic by about 0.2 percentage points a year, adding up to about one point over five years, and more optimistic the deeper the budget cuts the programme planned. On this map, the Yacyretá dam between Paraguay and Argentina saw its cost rise from $2.5 billion to over $10.5 billion, or over $15 billion by International Rivers' count.

An honest mistake and a deliberate one leave the same trace in a forecast, so the missing piece is intent. It would show in the working files: appraisal models and consultants' forecasts for large loan-financed projects, read beside the drafts they replaced and the outcomes that followed. The World Bank's evaluation office says the inside history of the 1992 task force is documented in the Bank's archives, and a count of how often forecasts were raised under deadline pressure would test whether the bias was pushed or simply drifted.
missing: No study has compared draft and final appraisal forecasts across the Bank's portfolio.
would_settle: Appraisal models and consultant forecasts for large loan-financed projects, compared draft against final and against outcomes, starting from the Portfolio Management Task Force files in the World Bank archives.

title: Lenders kept funding dictators they knew were stealing
conviction: Two leaked internal documents show lenders knew of large-scale theft; lending continued in both cases. How often this happened is the suspicion.
story: In 1982 a confidential report by a retired German central banker leaked from Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of Congo. Erwin Blumenthal had been sent by the IMF to run the country's central bank, and on Zaire's $4.1 billion foreign debt he wrote that there was "no - I repeat no - chance" the creditors would be repaid, because of the corruption of the people in power. The suspicion is that the big lenders often knew that the governments they were lending to were stealing, kept lending because those governments were useful allies, and then held ordinary people responsible for the debt.

Zaire's lending did not stop. Probe International counted that over the next six years the IMF lent Zaire $600 million, the World Bank $650 million and Western governments nearly $3 billion. When Mobutu Sese Seko was overthrown in 1997 the country owed more than $13 billion. In Indonesia, World Bank staff in Jakarta wrote a confidential memo in August 1997 estimating that at least 20 to 30 per cent of the government's development budget was diverted through informal payments to officials and politicians, that there was no basis to claim Bank projects lost less, and that there were reports of 50 to 80 per cent being taken from money meant for land purchase and resettlement. The month before, the Bank's vice-president for East Asia, Jean-Michel Severino, had said: "We know exactly where our money is going." The memo became public only when the Wall Street Journal obtained it in 1998.

The Philippines shows who pays. Under Ferdinand Marcos, Westinghouse built the Bataan nuclear plant, which cost about $2.3 billion, was finished in 1984 and never produced electricity. Westinghouse admitted paying $17.2 million to a Marcos associate, Herminio Disini, which it called a legitimate commission, and a US jury acquitted the company of bribery in 1993. In 2021 the Philippine Supreme Court held Disini liable for using undue influence to win Westinghouse the contract. Filipinos finished paying the plant's loans in April 2007, a total of 64.7 billion pesos in principal and interest. There is an old idea in international law, odious debt, that debts a regime takes on against its own people should not bind them, but it has rarely been applied.

Lenders do not have to publish what their staff knew when a loan was approved, and the two documents above surfaced only through leaks. What would settle the suspicion are the internal country risk assessments and board papers for lending to Zaire, Indonesia and the Philippines in those years, and to other long-ruling allies, many of which are now old enough to request from the lenders' archives.
missing: No systematic review of lender archives for internal warnings of theft before continued lending.
would_settle: Internal country risk assessments and board papers for lending to Zaire, Indonesia and the Philippines in the 1970s to 1990s, requested from the World Bank and IMF archives.

countries.note: Blumenthal report 1982; lending continued; debt over $13 billion by 1997.

title: Aid money turns up in Swiss bank accounts
conviction: One peer-reviewed study, partly by a World Bank economist, measures the leak. Who moved the money, and why the Bank held the paper, are the suspicion.
story: When the World Bank pays money to a very poor country, it is meant for roads, salaries and clinics. The suspicion is that a measurable slice goes straight into private bank accounts in tax havens such as Switzerland, belonging to the people who control the government, and that the Bank tried to keep the evidence quiet. If so, part of every aid payment to the most aid-dependent countries is helping the people in power get richer, which gives them less reason to fix anything.

In 2020 three economists, Jørgen Juel Andersen, Niels Johannesen and the World Bank's own Bob Rijkers, compared World Bank aid payments to the 22 most aid-dependent countries with bank deposits recorded by the Bank for International Settlements, the central banks' own bank. In the quarters when a country received aid worth 1 per cent of its national income, its deposits in offshore centres known for bank secrecy rose by 3.4 per cent. Its deposits in ordinary financial centres did not move. That works out to about 7.5 per cent of the aid leaking out, and more the more a country depends on aid. Among the havens it could trace country by country, Switzerland was by far the most important, and the rise was driven by accounts in Switzerland and Luxembourg. The paper later passed peer review and was published in the Journal of Political Economy in 2022.

What happened to the paper is part of the story. The Economist reported that it passed the Bank's internal review in November 2019 but that higher officials blocked publication. The Bank's chief economist, Pinelopi Goldberg, resigned after less than 15 months in the job, and The Economist linked her departure to the paper. Johannesen, a professor in Copenhagen who did not work for the Bank, then posted the draft on his own website, and within hours the Bank published it as one of its working papers. The method cannot say who opened the accounts or who moved the money, only that the deposits rose when the aid arrived.

The deposit figures are country totals, so they show that money moved but not whose money it was. What would settle it is account-level information: records from the haven banks of deposits from officials in the weeks after aid was paid out, which tax authorities can now obtain under information-exchange treaties. Two further records would help: the Bank's internal correspondence on why the paper was held, and the same test run on IMF lending, regional development banks and individual donor governments.
missing: The same method has not been applied to IMF, regional bank or bilateral donor disbursements. No account-level records are public.
would_settle: Account-level haven deposit records matched to disbursement dates; the World Bank's internal correspondence on the paper's review; the method rerun on other lenders.

countries.note: By far the most important haven among those with country-level data; with Luxembourg, drove the rise.
Highest aid-to-GDP ratio in the study's sample (33.5 per cent), per ProMarket.

title: Rescue loans that rescue the banks, not the country
conviction: Leaked IMF board minutes and a line-by-line study of where the Greek money went. Whether rescues are designed this way as a rule is the suspicion.
story: On 9 May 2010 the IMF's board met in Washington to approve its share of a €110 billion rescue for Greece. The minutes were marked strictly confidential. The suspicion is that big rescue loans are designed first to pay foreign private banks back in full, moving their losses onto the borrowing country's taxpayers and the governments that lend, while the country itself gets years of cuts. If so, the word rescue describes who was saved wrongly.

The minutes reached the Wall Street Journal in 2013. Brazil's director told the board the programme might be seen not as a rescue of Greece but as a bailout of Greece's private debt holders, mainly European financial institutions. Directors for Argentina, Brazil, India, Russia and Switzerland said it was missing a reduction of Greece's debt to private lenders. The Dutch, French and German directors told the board their countries' banks would broadly keep their holdings of Greek debt. According to The Press Project, banks from those three countries held more than $122 billion of Greek government bonds early in 2010 and began selling that spring. In June 2013 the IMF's managing director, Christine Lagarde, said that in May 2010 the Fund had not known Greece would need its debt restructured.

In 2016 the European School of Management and Technology in Berlin traced where the money went. Of €215.9 billion paid out in Greece's first two programmes, €86.9 billion repaid old debts, €52.3 billion paid interest and €37.3 billion recapitalised Greek banks. Only €9.7 billion, less than 5 per cent, went into the Greek budget for anything else. The study's authors also blamed years of high Greek public spending, and other analysts count the same money differently. On this map, the 2012 Greek programme cut the minimum wage by 22 per cent.

Some of the most important records are still not public. What would settle the question are the full IMF staff papers behind the 2010 programme, the European Central Bank's records of which Greek bonds it bought and from whom, and the exposure reports of the named banks month by month in 2010. Together they would show whether the programme was shaped around getting particular creditors out before the losses fell.
missing: The ECB's bond-purchase counterparty records and month-by-month bank exposure data for 2010 have not been obtained.
would_settle: Full IMF staff papers for the 2010 Greek arrangement; ECB records of Greek bond purchases by counterparty; month-by-month 2010 exposure reports of the French, German and Dutch banks.

countries.note: Less than 5 per cent of €215.9 billion reached the budget for other uses.

title: The lenders expect the riots their conditions cause
conviction: A leaked World Bank strategy, a count of 146 protests and a global study linking adjustment loans to repression. Whether the lenders plan for repression is the suspicion.
story: On 25 June 2024 Kenya's parliament passed a finance bill full of new taxes, and protesters forced their way into the parliament building. Police opened fire. Kenya's state-funded human rights commission later said police had killed at least 60 people. Human Rights Watch reported that the bill was meant to raise an extra $2.3 billion, in part to meet IMF revenue requirements. The suspicion is that the lenders know, before they set conditions like these, that prices will rise, people will protest and governments will use force, and that they write this into their plans as an acceptable cost.

There is a paper trail. In 2001 Joseph Stiglitz, a former World Bank chief economist, described the "IMF riot" to the reporter Greg Palast as one of the steps of a lending programme. Palast's team at the Observer and the BBC obtained confidential World Bank documents, among them an interim strategy for Ecuador which said, more than once, that the plans could be expected to spark social unrest, and which called for meeting it with political resolve.

Researchers have counted what follows. In their 1994 book Free Markets and Food Riots, John Walton and David Seddon listed 146 protests against austerity in 39 debtor countries between 1976 and 1992. A global study by Rodwan Abouharb and David Cingranelli covering 1981 to 2000, which allowed for the fact that troubled countries are more likely to get such loans in the first place, found that carrying out a World Bank structural adjustment agreement worsened governments' respect for freedom from torture, political imprisonment, killings by the state and disappearances. This map holds cases of the same shape: the Caracazo in Venezuela in 1989, where the card counts 276 dead after fuel prices rose, and Ecuador in October 2019, where ending fuel subsidies more than doubled prices and 11 people died. The documented pattern on this map, the money kept flowing after the killings, shows that the lending usually continued.

The planning documents are usually confidential, and the Ecuador strategy came out through a leak. Lenders do not count deaths that follow their programmes. What would settle the question is a count across published IMF staff reports and World Bank programme documents of how often the risk sections predicted unrest before a big price rise, and whether the plan changed when they did. Many of those documents are now public after the fact, so the count can be done.
missing: No count of risk sections in IMF and World Bank programme documents that forecast unrest.
would_settle: A count of IMF staff reports and World Bank programme documents whose risk sections forecast unrest before major price increases, with whether the programme changed.

title: Global rankings bent for countries with money to give
conviction: A law firm's investigation found the rankings were changed for China and Saudi Arabia. Whether this was routine is the suspicion.
story: For almost 20 years the World Bank published Doing Business, which ranked 190 countries on how easy they made it to start and run a company. Investors used it to decide where to put money, and governments rewrote their laws to climb it. The suspicion is that the rankings were adjusted for countries the Bank needed or that were paying it, and that the scoring itself pushed countries to remove protections for workers.

In September 2021 the law firm WilmerHale reported the results of an investigation it ran for the Bank. It found that staff changed China's data under pressure from the office of the Bank's president, Jim Yong Kim, and from its chief executive, Kristalina Georgieva, at a time when the Bank was seeking China's support for a large increase in its capital. The changes put China at 78th in the 2018 edition, seven places higher than the draft data had it. According to the report, Georgieva visited a manager's home to collect the final printed copy and thanked the employee for helping to resolve the problem. She said she disagreed fundamentally with the findings, and the IMF's board, where she had become managing director, backed her in October 2021. For the 2020 edition, the report found that senior staff changed Saudi Arabia's data. Saudi Arabia rose 30 places to 62nd and was named the top improver. It had paid the Bank for advisory work aimed at improving the very indicators being scored. WilmerHale found no evidence that the president's office or the board were involved in the 2020 changes. The Bank cancelled Doing Business.

There had been warnings. In January 2018 the Bank's chief economist, Paul Romer, said Chile had fallen in the rankings because of changes in method rather than in Chile, and suggested politics might be behind it. He then said he had not meant to suggest manipulation, and resigned; Augusto Lopez-Claros, who had directed the group that published the rankings, called the claim that the changes targeted Chile wholly without merit. The rankings also shaped laws. In 2006 Saudi Arabia's king said he wanted the country among the top ten by 2010. Until 2009 the ranking scored countries higher for weaker worker protections, through what it called the employing workers indicator. The Bank suspended that indicator in 2009 after pressure from unions, the International Labour Organization and the US Congress, and an independent panel the Bank set up in 2013 recommended removing it permanently.

WilmerHale examined two editions. What would settle whether China and Saudi Arabia were exceptions is the full record of original and final data for every country in every edition from 2003, with each change and who asked for it. The Bank's new Business Ready ranking, launched in 2024, brings a labour topic back, so the same record matters again.
missing: The full data change log across all Doing Business editions has not been published.
would_settle: Original and final data for every country in every Doing Business edition, 2003 to 2020, with each change and its requester.

title: Secret loans arranged by banks and traders, kept from the public
conviction: A bank's guilty plea, debts revealed overnight in Congo and Chad, and $385 billion of underreported Chinese-linked debt. That hidden lending is routine is the suspicion.
story: In the port of Maputo, Mozambique, a fleet of tuna boats bought with borrowed money has sat rusting for years. The loans behind them were kept secret from Mozambique's parliament and from the IMF. The suspicion is that this is not unusual: that arranging hidden loans is ordinary business for some international banks and commodity traders, and that the public finds out only when the country can no longer pay. If so, the debt figures that the IMF and World Bank publish, and use to set conditions, are often wrong from the start.

In 2013 and 2014 three companies linked to Mozambique's state borrowed about $2 billion through Credit Suisse and Russia's VTB for the tuna fleet and coastal security. The Financial Times reported that the deals had been inflated from $300 million to over $2 billion. US authorities said about $200 million went in bribes and kickbacks: about $150 million to Mozambican officials and about $50 million to Credit Suisse bankers. In 2021 Credit Suisse admitted fraud, agreed to pay about $475 million to US and UK authorities, and cancelled $200 million of Mozambique's debt. A study by Mozambique's Centre for Public Integrity and Norway's Chr. Michelsen Institute put the cost to the economy at $11 billion and found the slowdown pushed nearly two million people into poverty.

In the Republic of Congo, the commodity traders Glencore and Trafigura had lent the government money repaid in future oil. In 2017 the IMF raised its estimate of Congo's debt from 77 to 110 per cent of national income after hidden debts came to light; Debt Justice said it could not tell how much of the jump was hidden debt and how much was falling output or new loans. Global Witness later found the state oil company carrying up to $3.3 billion more that had never been disclosed. In Chad, Glencore held 98 per cent of the government's foreign commercial debt by the end of 2016, and in 2016 $231 million of the government's $271 million in net oil revenue, about 85 per cent, went to Glencore. In 2021 AidData found about $385 billion of debt linked to Chinese lending that poorer governments had not reported, mostly because it was owed by state companies and special-purpose firms rather than the government itself. In Europe, Goldman Sachs arranged currency swaps for Greece in 2001 that hid about €2.8 billion of debt, after Greece had joined the euro. Goldman said the swaps were legal under the rules of the time.

These debts stay hidden because the World Bank's debt register relies on what governments choose to report, loans to state companies are often left out, and trader prepayment deals are private contracts. AidData found the size of the gap for Chinese lending by comparing what lenders recorded with what borrowers reported. Nobody has done the same for Western banks and commodity traders, and doing so country by country would show how much of the world's debt is missing from the official numbers.
missing: No creditor-side comparison has been made for Western banks and commodity traders as AidData did for Chinese lenders.
would_settle: A country-by-country comparison of creditor-side records (bank and trader filings, BIS data) with debtor reports to the World Bank Debtor Reporting System.

title: Rescue money timed to keep friendly governments in power
conviction: Three rescues arrived just before elections, with one US official's reported admission and one president's public condition. Whether this is a regular practice is the suspicion.
story: On 14 October 2025, twelve days before Argentina's midterm elections, Donald Trump sat beside Argentina's president, Javier Milei, at the White House and talked about the $20 billion the US Treasury had just made available to Argentina. "If he loses, we are not going to be generous with Argentina," he said. The suspicion is that the biggest powers behind the lenders time and size rescue money to keep friendly governments in office. If so, voters in borrowing countries are choosing under a threat they may not see.

Argentina had been here before. In June 2018 the IMF approved the largest loan in its history for the government of Mauricio Macri, raised in October to $57 billion, equal to 1,227 per cent of Argentina's quota at the Fund, a year before Macri ran for re-election. In July 2020 Mauricio Claver-Carone, Trump's adviser on Latin America, was reported to have told a teleconference held by the Chilean Council on Foreign Relations that Trump asked the IMF for the loan so that Macri would win the election; Argentine senators repeated the account in a letter that November. The IMF's own 2021 review found that the programme did not meet its objectives. Only four of its twelve planned reviews were completed, and Macri lost. In 2025 the US Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, said the new support was tied to policy, not to the election. Milei's party won about 41 per cent of the vote.

Russia in 1996 had the same shape. In February the IMF agreed a $10.2 billion loan to Boris Yeltsin's government, four months before he faced the Communist candidate, Gennady Zyuganov. The IMF's managing director said the Fund was not taking sides; Zyuganov called the loan political. The Economist claimed that summer that the IMF and the Russian government had worked together to keep Russia within the loan conditions on paper, and after the election the IMF held back a payment. A study of 157 countries from 1999 to 2005 by the economist Axel Dreher and colleagues found that countries voting with the United States at the UN General Assembly received lower inflation forecasts from the IMF as their elections approached. This map's documented pattern on aid and UN votes shows the same pull on aid.

The instructions that the US Treasury gives its director on the IMF board are not published, and board minutes are confidential for years. What would settle the question are those instructions and minutes for the 1996 and 2018 loans, and a count across all IMF programmes of approvals and payments in the months before elections, set against how closely each government votes with the largest shareholders.
missing: No count of IMF approvals and disbursements before elections, split by political alignment with major shareholders.
would_settle: US Treasury voting instructions and IMF board minutes for the 1996 Russian and 2018 Argentine arrangements; a count of pre-election approvals and disbursements across all IMF programmes by voting alignment.

countries.note: $57 billion in 2018; $20 billion swap before the October 2025 vote.
$10.2 billion four months before Yeltsin's re-election.

title: Chinese-financed ports that may be future naval bases
conviction: One base opened after years of denial, a second facility hosting Chinese warships, and a researched shortlist of eight more. That port lending is laying the ground for bases is the suspicion.
story: For years China said it had no plans for a military base in Djibouti, on the Horn of Africa. It confirmed one in November 2015 and opened it in 2017. The suspicion is that some of the ports China has paid for or built around the world were planned with a second purpose: places where its navy could dock, refuel and one day be based, with the loans giving Beijing the leverage to ask. If so, a country taking a Chinese loan for a harbour may also be signing up, without saying so, to a side in a future conflict.

Cambodia's Ream naval base is the case being watched. In 2019 the Wall Street Journal reported an agreement giving China's navy use of the base for 30 years; both governments denied it. China paid to rebuild Ream, and satellite images showed a new pier almost identical to the one at Djibouti and long enough to berth Chinese aircraft carriers. Two Chinese warships berthed there from December 2023. Cambodia formally opened the rebuilt Ream in April 2025 and declared it open to foreign navies, and a US warship visited in early 2026. In 2023 AidData counted 123 Chinese-financed seaport projects at 78 ports in 46 countries, worth $29.9 billion, and named the eight most likely places for China's next bases: Hambantota in Sri Lanka, Bata in Equatorial Guinea, Gwadar in Pakistan, Kribi in Cameroon, Ream, Luganville in Vanuatu, Nacala in Mozambique and Nouakchott in Mauritania. It also noted that none of them is currently militarily defensible.

One famous version of this story does not hold. Hambantota is often described as a port China seized when Sri Lanka could not pay. Research for Chatham House found otherwise: the 2017 99-year lease to China Merchants Port was a new investment of $1.12 billion, not a swap of debt for the port, the Chinese loans for the port were only 4.8 per cent of the government's foreign debt, and Sri Lanka got no debt relief from it. So the suspicion is not a debt trap. It is that commercial ports are being chosen and built so they can serve a navy too. On this map, Hambantota's industrial zone met protests over the taking of village and farm land, and Gwadar's port and new expressway have pushed fishers off their homes and fishing routes.

The port contracts and loan agreements are mostly unpublished, which is where any clause giving warships access would sit. What would settle the question is publication of those contracts, and the records of which naval vessels call at the eight shortlisted ports over the coming years. Repeated long stays by Chinese warships would confirm the suspicion; their absence would weaken it.
missing: Port concession and loan contracts for the eight shortlisted ports are unpublished; no consolidated log of naval port calls.
would_settle: Publication of the concession and loan contracts for the shortlisted ports; naval port-call records for those ports over time.

title: Poor countries chosen to take rich countries' toxic waste
conviction: A World Bank memo set out the logic and a commodity trader's ship followed it. Whether waste flows follow that logic as a rule is the suspicion.
story: On the night of 19 August 2006, lorries began dumping black liquid at rubbish tips and roadsides around Abidjan, the largest city in Côte d'Ivoire. It was waste from the Probo Koala, a ship chartered by the oil trader Trafigura. The suspicion is that companies, and some of the economists who advise the big lenders, treat people in poor countries as cheaper to poison, and that hazardous waste travels to where harming people costs least.

The logic was written down 15 years earlier. A memo dated 12 December 1991 went out under the name of Lawrence Summers, then the World Bank's chief economist. It argued that health-damaging pollution should be done where its cost was lowest, which meant the country with the lowest wages, and it called the economic logic of dumping a load of toxic waste in the lowest-wage country "impeccable". The memo was actually written by a Bank economist, Lant Pritchett. Both men said it was meant as sarcasm, and Pritchett said the leaked version had been doctored to remove context. It was leaked in February 1992 by Friends of the Earth to the Brazilian newspaper Jornal do Brasil, and Brazil's environment secretary, José Lutzenberger, replied that the reasoning was logical and insane.

The Probo Koala had tried to unload its waste in Amsterdam in July 2006 and taken it back on board. In Abidjan a newly licensed local firm, Compagnie Tommy, was hired to get rid of more than 500 tonnes for about $17,000. More than 100,000 people sought medical help. A national inquiry recorded 15 deaths and an Ivorian court 17. In 2007 Trafigura paid the government about $198 million in a settlement that ended prosecution, without admitting wrongdoing; in 2009 it paid £30 million to about 30,000 people who had sued in London, again without admitting liability. In 2010 a Dutch court fined it €1 million for concealing how dangerous the waste was. Trafigura has always said the waste could not have caused deaths or serious injury.

Shipments like this are often hidden by calling waste something else, such as a ship's slops or goods for recycling. Countries that have signed the Basel Convention, the treaty on hazardous waste, report their exports each year. Matching those reports against the wages and the waste-treatment capacity of the countries receiving the waste would show whether the trade follows the memo's logic or not.
missing: No analysis matching Basel Convention export reports to destination wages and treatment capacity.
would_settle: Basel Convention national reports on hazardous waste exports, matched to destination-country wages and treatment capacity.

title: Markets forced open for rich countries' subsidized food
conviction: A former US president's apology, a reversed tariff in Ghana and the collapse of local farming in both. Whether lending conditions are written for rich-country exporters is the suspicion.
story: In March 2010, two months after the earthquake that destroyed much of Port-au-Prince, Bill Clinton told the US Senate that a policy he had pushed in Haiti in the 1990s had been a mistake. "It may have been good for some of my farmers in Arkansas," he said, but it had cost Haiti its ability to grow its own rice. The suspicion is that the conditions attached to loans, telling poor countries to cut tariffs on food imports, were written to open markets for farm exporters in rich countries, whose governments pay them large subsidies, and that local farmers paid the price.

In 1995, under a programme run with the IMF and the World Bank, Haiti cut its tariff on imported rice to 3 per cent, a year after Clinton had restored President Jean-Bertrand Aristide to power. Haiti now buys more than 80 per cent of its rice from the United States. Between 1995 and 2011, according to the Environmental Working Group, Arkansas farmers received more than $2 billion in direct federal payments, half of it for rice.

Ghana tells the same story with chickens. Imports of chicken rose from 26,000 tonnes in 2002 to about 40,000 tonnes in 2004, and local farmers' share of their own market fell from 95 per cent in 1992 to 11 per cent in 2002. In 2003 Ghana's parliament voted to double the tariff on imported poultry to 40 per cent. The government backed down within two months, under pressure from the IMF according to press reports, and Inter Press Service reported that the European Union's trade commissioner, Pascal Lamy, had lobbied against the tariff. The EU pays its own farmers about €43 billion a year. In Mexico, after the 1994 NAFTA trade deal removed protection for corn farmers, farm employment fell from 8.1 million in 1993 to 6.8 million in 2001, though the source attributes most of that fall to other causes, such as migration to cities, land reforms and Mexico's own earlier cuts to corn price supports, and finds NAFTA played only a minor role. This map's documented pattern on tied aid shows the same direction of travel: much of the money goes back to companies in the donor country.

The loan conditions are public; the reasons behind them are not. What would settle the question is a country-by-country comparison of the food-tariff cuts written into IMF and World Bank programmes with which rich countries' exporters gained market share afterwards, read beside the negotiating records, such as the instructions the US and EU gave their directors on those programmes.
missing: No country-by-country comparison of lender-required tariff cuts with subsequent export gains by rich-country suppliers.
would_settle: Food-tariff conditions in IMF and World Bank programmes matched to post-programme import shares by supplier country, read with US and EU instructions to their executive directors.

title: Carbon credits driving a new land grab
conviction: Agreements covering a fifth of Zimbabwe and a tenth of Liberia and Zambia, a court ruling against Kenya's largest soil-carbon project, and evictions rights groups have linked to carbon deals. That carbon finance is driving evictions is the suspicion.
story: On 2 November 2023, the Kenyan government began evicting the Ogiek, an Indigenous people who have lived in the Mau Forest for generations, from their homes at Sasimwani. Survival International counted about 167 houses destroyed, including a school. A few weeks earlier Kenya had signed an agreement with a Dubai company, Blue Carbon, to produce carbon credits on millions of hectares. The suspicion is that the market in carbon credits, which lets companies pay for forests to be protected so they can count that against their own emissions, is driving a new land grab in poor countries, in which governments sign huge areas over to foreign firms and the people living there are fenced out.

Blue Carbon was set up in 2022 and is chaired by a member of Dubai's ruling family, Sheikh Ahmed Dalmook Al Maktoum. During 2023 it signed agreements covering about a fifth of Zimbabwe (7.5 million hectares), about a tenth of Zambia (8 million hectares), 8 million hectares of Tanzania's forest reserves and about a tenth of Liberia (around 1 million hectares). Altogether that was an area about the size of the United Kingdom. Under the leaked Liberian agreement, the company would take 70 per cent of the income for the first ten years. Liberia's government later said its deal had been stopped, and an AFP investigation in 2025 found that other deals had also gone nowhere. Amnesty International, Minority Rights Group and Survival International put out a joint statement asking whether carbon credits were behind the Ogiek evictions. The government said it was protecting the environment, and Blue Carbon told the BBC it had no ongoing projects in Kenya.

In northern Kenya, the Northern Rangelands Trust runs a soil-carbon project covering more than 2 million hectares across 14 community conservancies, selling credits to companies including Netflix and Meta. In January 2025 a Kenyan court ruled that two of its largest conservancies had been set up unconstitutionally, with no basis in law; one of them produced about a fifth of the project's credits. Verra, the main body that certifies carbon credits, suspended the project in 2023 and again in 2025, and reinstated it in 2026. This map holds earlier cases of the same kind: the Sengwer evicted from Embobut Forest in 2014, and carbon projects in Peru, Cambodia, Kenya and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Most carbon agreements between governments and companies are not published, and Liberia's became known only because it leaked. What would settle the question is the full set of carbon-rights agreements signed since 2020, together with the registries of certified projects, checked against court records and documented evictions in the same areas. A count of how many registered land-based carbon projects overlap with evictions would show whether the cases here are exceptions or the pattern.
missing: No count of registered land-based carbon projects overlapping documented evictions.
would_settle: All government carbon-rights agreements since 2020 and carbon registry project boundaries, checked against court records and documented evictions.

countries.note: Ogiek evictions November 2023; two NRT conservancies ruled unconstitutional in 2025.
